opus-5.5.text:
I think they're more connected than people usually assume. When you do research at the frontier, you're dealing with something that doesn't exist yet. Nobody can give you the answer, and often nobody can even tell you whether the question is the right one. Managing a team that's trying to do that is very different from managing a team executing a known plan.

In a traditional organization, you can break the goal into pieces, assign them, and measure progress against a roadmap. With new knowledge, the roadmap is mostly a guess. So the manager's job shifts. It's less about control and more about creating conditions where the right ideas can emerge and survive. You have to tolerate a lot of uncertainty, and you have to be willing to let people pursue directions that look unpromising at first, because some breakthroughs only make sense in hindsight.

There's also a feedback loop. How you organize people shapes what kind of knowledge you can produce. If the team is very hierarchical, you tend to get incremental improvements on whatever the top person already believes. If information flows freely and people feel safe challenging each other, including challenging me, you get a better chance of finding something truly new. In a way the organization is itself a kind of model. Its structure determines what it can learn.

So I often think about the team the way I'd think about a research problem. What are the right priors? Where should we spend compute, meaning people's time and attention? How do we make sure we're actually learning from experiments, including failed ones, rather than just confirming what we hoped? A lot of the principles of good research, like being honest about results, focusing on what really matters, and staying close to first principles, turn out to be principles of good management too.

And personally, I don't see them as two separate jobs. If I only manage and stop thinking about the technical problems, I lose the judgment needed to make good decisions. If I only do research and ignore the organization, the work can't scale. The interesting part is holding both at once.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're much more connected than people usually assume. When you do research, the core thing you're really doing is managing uncertainty. You have a problem nobody has solved, you don't know which direction will work, and you have to allocate your limited attention across several possible paths, kill the ones that aren't working, and double down on the ones that show signal. Running a team is the same process at a different scale. Instead of allocating your own hours, you're allocating people, compute, and time, and instead of one brain exploring the hypothesis space, you have many.

So in a sense, a research lab is itself a kind of scientific instrument. The design of the organization determines what questions it can answer. If information flows slowly, if people are afraid to report negative results, if incentives push everyone toward safe incremental work, then the instrument has a very narrow bandwidth, and you'll never see the surprising things. A lot of what I think about as a manager is really epistemics: how do we make sure the truth about what's working travels fast, how do we keep the team honest when an idea we all love turns out to be wrong, how do we keep enough slack in the system that someone can chase a strange observation for two weeks without having to justify it.

The other connection is taste. In research, the hardest part isn't execution, it's choosing the problem. Most of the value comes from a small number of correct bets on what matters. Managing a team forces you to make that taste explicit, because you have to communicate it to people and convince them. That process actually sharpens your own understanding. When I have to explain to twenty people why we're betting on scaling a particular direction, I discover the holes in my reasoning much faster than when it's just in my head.

And there's a feedback loop in the other direction too. Creating new knowledge changes what the team needs to be. Once you understand something, the organization has to reconfigure around that insight, which means management isn't a fixed skill you apply once, it's a continuous response to what you're learning. So I don't really see them as two jobs. I see one job, which is building a system that discovers truth faster than it otherwise would, and sometimes that system is a model and sometimes it's a group of people.

astra-6.text:
I think managing a team and creating new scientific knowledge are closely connected, because research depends on how people make decisions under uncertainty. You don’t know in advance which idea will work, so you can’t manage it entirely as a sequence of predictable deliverables.

The important thing is to give people a shared understanding of the problem, while leaving room for them to challenge assumptions and explore different approaches. You need enough coordination that people can build on each other’s work, but enough independence that everyone doesn’t end up making the same bet.

There’s also a feedback loop. A scientific insight can change what the team should focus on, and how you organize the team can affect which insights become possible. So I see management as part of the research process: creating an environment where people can take intellectual risks, test ideas carefully, and change direction when the evidence tells them to.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re closely connected, because the way you organize a team shapes the questions it can explore. Research needs room for uncertainty. If every project has to produce a predictable result on a fixed schedule, people will naturally choose safer problems, and you may miss opportunities to discover something new.

At the same time, giving people freedom doesn’t mean having no structure. You need a shared understanding of which questions matter, clear communication, and a way to learn from experiments that don’t work. As a manager, part of your job is to help people challenge assumptions—including your own—and make sure evidence carries more weight than seniority.

So I see management as creating the conditions for discovery. You can’t plan the scientific insight itself, but you can build a team that is better able to recognize and pursue it.
